s7-name~idea.cta: How does it begin? on the Sentence road
s7-name~idea.title: How does it begin?
s7-name~idea.body: Most sentences start with the subject. Good writers also open with an adverb (Suddenly, Slowly), a prepositional phrase (Behind the hut, At the end of the day), an -ing phrase (Seeing who it was) or a subordinate clause (When…, If…, As soon as…). A clause has its own subject and verb; a phrase does not.
s7-name~idea.more: I can name the way a writer opens a sentence.

s7-name~story.cta: How does it begin? on the Sentence road
s7-name~story.title: How does it begin?

s7-vary~idea.cta: Vary the start on the Sentence road
s7-vary~idea.title: Vary the start
s7-vary~idea.body: When every sentence starts with the subject, a paragraph plods like footsteps. Move a part to the front — a time, a place, a how, a reason — and the rhythm wakes up. Put a comma after a longer opening, before the main clause begins.

li7-genre~idea.cta: Which shelf? on the Literature road
li7-genre~idea.title: Which shelf?
li7-genre~idea.body: A genre is a family of stories that share features. A fable is short, has animals that talk, and ends with a moral. A fairy tale has magic and wonder. An adventure has journeys and danger. A mystery has a puzzle or a crime to solve from clues. Fantasy builds an impossible world. A play is written to be acted, with speakers' names before their lines. A speech is spoken aloud to an audience.
li7-genre~idea.more: I can tell an adventure from a mystery, and name other genres.

la7-devices~idea.cta: Four tricks of great speakers on the Language road
la7-devices~idea.title: Four tricks of great speakers
la7-devices~idea.body: Anaphora: the same words begin several clauses in a row ("we cannot… we cannot…"). Tricolon: a group of three, built alike ("of the people, by the people, for the people"). Alliteration: words close together begin with the same sound ("the furrow followed free"). A rhetorical question is asked for effect, not for an answer.
la7-devices~idea.more: I can name anaphora, tricolon, alliteration and a rhetorical question.

la7-antithesis~idea.cta: Antithesis, and the whole toolkit on the Language road
la7-antithesis~idea.title: Antithesis, and the whole toolkit
la7-antithesis~idea.body: Antithesis sets opposites side by side in matching shapes: "living and dead", "not with the eyes, but with the mind". The balance makes the contrast ring. Great speeches often stack devices — a tricolon whose parts begin alike is also anaphora — so ask which device the line shows most clearly.
la7-antithesis~idea.more: I can name antithesis, and tell it from anaphora and tricolon.

la7-antithesis~story.cta: Antithesis, and the whole toolkit on the Language road
la7-antithesis~story.title: Antithesis, and the whole toolkit
la7-antithesis~story.body: Quill reads Frederick Douglass aloud and stops, struck: "You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man." Two halves, the words swapped, the meaning turned upside down. That is antithesis.
